newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Union bodies say SKorea reneging on labour reform.
newsitem.headline: Union bodies say SKorea reneging on labour reform.

text.p: International trade union groupings voiced alarm on Thursday over what they said was mounting labour tension in South Korea and accused the Seoul government of rowing back on commitments to reform labour laws.

In separate letters to President Kim Young-sam, leaders of two major union federations based in Geneva made clear that they would work to stop South Korea's admission to the Paris-based OECD "rich man's club" unless reform went ahead.

Officials of the two bodies, representing 30 million metalworkers and private service-sector workers around the globe, also said they feared police could take violent action to break up a workers' rally planned for Seoul on Saturday.

"As you are well aware, the situation is critical," Philip Jennings, General Secretary of the white-collar workers' federation FIET, told Kim in his letter, a copy of which was made available to news agencies.

Marcello Malentacchi, General Secretary of the International Metalworkers' Federation (IMWF), expressed "grave concern" to the South Korean leader over the apparent failure of a presidential commission to agree on radical labour reform.

Both said the president of the Korean Confederation of Trade Unions (KCTU), Kwon Young-kil, had begun an indefinite hunger strike this week in a protest over alleged government and employer efforts to bring in more stringent labour laws.

Kwon served a term in prison earlier this year for labour activities, bringing criticism for Seoul from the United Nations' International Labour Organisation (ILO) whose conventions on worker freedoms it has signed.

The presidential commission, from which the recently-formed KCTU has withdrawn over lack of progress, was set up in May, apparently as part of South Korea's bid to win admission to the OECD -- the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development.

Members of the grouping -- until now mainly Western industrial powers -- have urged reform of South Korea's restrictive labour laws, left over from the authoritarian and military regimes which ruled the country for decades, to ease entry.
Last month a formal invitation was issued to Seoul, which would be the first Asian "tiger" economy to come in, after it pledged to ensure basic freedoms laid out by the ILO.
These include the right to collective bargaining and the right to association, or to join a union of one's choice.

But Malentacchi, to whose federation the KCTU which was long refused recognition by the South Korean government, said in his letter that the presidential commission was apparently not even looking at either of these points.

He said he understood it was considering a ban on the use of the term "trade union" by non-registered unions, as well as extending the category of "essential services" in which industrial action is barred to the communications sector.

"It is clear that such proposals, if enacted, would significantly worsen the current position in respect of workers' rights and do nothing to deal with the unacceptable restriction of union pluralism," he told the South Korean president.

In his letter, the FIET's Jennings said that following what he described as the "violent dispersal" by police of a bank workers' demonstration in Seoul last weekend he feared bloodshed if Saturday's KCTU rally were also broken up.
"We urge the (South) Korean government to respect the rights of KCTU members to rally," he told Kim. "We also urge you to influence the police authorities to exercise necessary restraint."
